:::{#def-orthogonal-inner-product}
#### Orthogonality in an inner product space

In an inner product space (@def-inner-product-space)
with inner product $\iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}$,
two vectors $\vx$ and $\vy$ are **orthogonal with respect to** $\iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}$,
written $\vx \perp \vy$, if

$$\iprod{\vx}{\vy} = 0$$

[@banerjee2014linear, Definition 7.3, p. 181].
With the dot product as the inner product (@exm-dot-product-inner-product),
this condition is orthogonality as in @def-orthogonal-vectors.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-orthogonal-inner-product}
#### Orthogonality depends on the inner product

Take the weighted inner product of @exm-weighted-inner-product
with $\vecf{c} = (2, 1)$,
and let $\vx = (1, 2)$ and $\vy = (1, -1)$.
Then

$$
\ba
\iprod{\vx}{\vy}_{\vecf{c}}
&= 2 \cd 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 2 \cd (-1)
&& \text{(definition of } \iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\vecf{c}} \text{)}
\\
&= 2 - 2
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 0,
&& \text{(subtract)}
\ea
$$

so $\vx$ and $\vy$ are orthogonal with respect to $\iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\vecf{c}}$.
They are not orthogonal with respect to the dot product,
since

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vx \cdot \vy &= 1 \cd 1 + 2 \cd (-1) \\
&= -1 \\
&\ne 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
